title: Beyond Markovian Drifts: Action-Biased Geometric Walks with Memory for Personalized Summarization
one_liner: Instead of guessing what each reader cares about from their latest click alone, Walk2Pers uses a memory of their whole history and their recent actions to pick which parts of a document matter most to them.
lead: Document summarization—picking out the parts of a text that matter—is personal. What one reader finds essential another skips. The hard part is that what a reader cares about changes over time: an investor checks stock news for different reasons in February than in October. Old summarizers either ignore history (they guess from the latest click) or squash it into a tiny compressed state (a few hidden numbers). Walk2Pers thinks of preference as a walk through a space of what a reader likes, where each step depends on what the reader just did. It tracks the full journey, not just the last step, and lets the reader's actions—what they clicked, what they skipped—bend the walk forward.

problem.h2: Why old summarizers stumble on personal taste
paras: A document is billions of characters; a summary is a few sentences. The choice of which sentences matters depends on who is reading. A sports journalist and a lawyer read the same court ruling differently. Worse, each reader's taste drifts: the same person might focus on risk in winter and opportunity in spring.

Old summarizers handle this badly. Some ignore history and predict only from the reader's most recent action—which article they clicked last. This misses the slow drift in taste. Others compress all of history into a tiny hidden state (a few dozen numbers), squashing away most details. Both miss the real pattern: a reader's interests are not random; they have momentum. If you cared about AI regulation last month, you likely still care this month, maybe slightly different in emphasis.

callout.html: Personalized summarization must track how a reader's values shift over time—not ignore the past, not compress it to a single guess, but hold it and use it.

paras: Walk2Pers changes how the system represents a reader's evolving preferences. Old systems either throw away history or crush it into a static vector. Walk2Pers keeps the full trajectory—the sequence of actions and clicks—and treats it as a walk through an abstract space of what-the-reader-cares-about. That walk is not memoryless; each new step depends on where you came from.
object.object: Preference representation from compressed hidden state to action-conditioned walk with memory.

hidden.h2: The preference walk: a hidden path through time
hidden.name: Preference trajectory through action space
paras: The paper measures and uses a hidden quantity: the trajectory of preferences over time, encoded as a sequence of walks through an abstract space. A walk is not a single vector (compressed); it is a path, where each step depends on what action the reader took at that moment. This is not obvious from the data; it is inferred from the sequence of clicks and skips.

Walk2Pers estimates this trajectory by learning an encoder that maps each reader's action history into a sequence of steps. Each step has two components: a magnitude (how far to go) and an orientation (which direction—continuing the old preference or turning toward something new). The dual memory lanes (reinforce and suppress) act as filters that clean up noise and emphasize real patterns.

heat.caption: Darker means more influence on the final summary; highlighted cells drive the personalization.

reads.html: The preference walk is just the reader's changing taste encoded as a sequence of steps. Each step records 'how much' and 'which way' the reader turned based on their latest click. The two memory lanes filter this to keep signal and drop noise.

The hidden quantity is the action-conditioned walk approximating a mathematical model (a first-order function that maps actions to preference shifts) in preference space. Magnitude and orientation decomposition allows the model to separate the strength of each shift from whether the reader is deepening into a topic or shifting to something different, because when these are coded as separate numbers, the model can learn how much to amplify each one during training—magnitude can increase when the click is strong and clear, orientation can shift sharply when the click is to a new category.

mechanism.h2: Why memory and action-conditioning fix the problem
paras: Old systems use only the most recent action (Markovian: the next state depends only on the current state, not history). The problem is that reader preferences do not reset every day. If someone has read five sports articles and one law article, the next article they see is likely law-adjacent, not a random jump. Ignoring the five is a blind spot.

Walk2Pers keeps the full history but does not burden it as a single vector. Instead, it treats each past action as a step in the direction of that reader's taste. The magnitude of each step captures 'how much does this action push the preference?' A click on a top story pushes harder than a scroll-past. The orientation captures 'toward something familiar or toward something different?' If the reader is going deeper into AI policy, the walk continues that path with a small shift toward something new. If they jump to climate, the walk rotates sharply.

The dual memory lanes prevent drift. One lane reinforces: 'if you liked AI twice, keep that activated.' The other suppresses: 'if you skipped climate five times, dampen climate outputs.' Without this, noise from a single accidental click would corrupt the walk. With it, the walk survives random one-off distractions and holds to real patterns.

Finally, a drift term lets the system respond to the summary request itself. If a reader asks 'summarize for me,' the system slightly pulls the walk in the direction of the request, not just the history. This is why the paper calls it 'action-biased': each action (past and present) biases the walk.

stages.s: Reader action history: clicks, skips, time stamps
Encode each action as a directional step
Apply magnitude and orientation to each step
Run through dual memory lanes (reinforce and suppress)
Add drift from the summary request
Final preference walk determines which sentences to pick

math.words: The preference state at each time step is updated by taking a previous state, adding a weighted step (magnitude times orientation), reinforcing with a memory, and suppressing unwanted directions.
math.equation: p_t = (1 - alpha) * p_prev + alpha * (mag_t * dir_t + mem_reinforce_t - mem_suppress_t + drift_request)
symbols: The preference state at time step t
The preference state from the previous time step
The learning rate for how much new actions update the state
The magnitude (strength) of the action at time t
The orientation (direction) of the action at time t
The reinforcement from previous clicks we liked
The suppression of directions we disliked
The small nudge from the summary request itself

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Action 1: reader clicks a sports article. mag=0.8 (strong click), dir=sports direction.
Action 2: reader skips law article. mag=0.2 (weak skip), dir=law direction.

math.note: The equation formalizes the intuition: past actions compound through (1 - alpha) carry-forward, new actions adjust by their magnitude and direction, and memory lanes filter out noise.

items.html: If a reader accidentally clicks a spam article, the memory lanes must suppress it or the whole walk corrupts. The dual memory (reinforce and suppress) helps, but a single dominant outlier click can still skew preference. This is why the memory suppression lane is critical.

The walk must process every past action in sequence. A reader with 500 clicks requires 500 steps to compute; with millions of readers, this gets slow. One fix is to compress very old clicks (e.g., from a year ago) into a single memory value instead of processing them step-by-step, which saves computation because fewer steps means fewer math operations, but loses fine detail about how those old clicks unfolded since the compressed value throws away the order and timing.

items.b: The drift term can override preference if the request is strong.
items.html: If a user explicitly requests 'give me tech news' but their history is all sports, the drift term must be tuned right or it will either override history entirely (not personalized) or be drowned out (not responsive).

When the memory lanes are calibrated, the walk survives random noise and holds signal. When the drift term is balanced, new requests do refine the walk without erasing it. Cross-domain tests show the walk generalizes: the learned patterns transfer to new readers and datasets.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small dataset: pick 10 example readers, each with 20 past clicks (labeled with category: sports, law, AI, etc.) and 5 new documents to summarize. Implement Walk2Pers in a hundred lines: encode each click as a directional step, run the update equation, and let the walk select which sentences from each document to include in the summary. Run it against a baseline that uses only the most recent click. The demo must show that a reader whose history is (click sports, click AI, click sports) gets a summary with sports and AI emphasis, not just sports emphasis from the latest click. The payoff is visible when the summary shifts smoothly as the reader's history shifts.
demo.metric_eq: Personalization match = (percentage of sentences the reader would have selected if asked) - (percentage the baseline got right)
demo.closing: A reader's taste is a journey, not a point. If the demo shows the journey, it has worked.
